summary: In the high priest’s courtyard, Peter three times denies knowing Jesus; the rooster crows, the Lord looks at him, and Peter goes out and weeps bitterly.
key_insight: Luke alone says that at the rooster’s crow “the Lord turned and looked at Peter.” Jesus was on trial for His life, and His attention went to the friend who had just denied Him. Peter wept because he remembered the word of the Lord.
story: Peter had followed Jesus at a distance. Another disciple, known to the high priest, spoke to the girl who kept the door and brought Peter into the courtyard. {Jn} It was cold, {Jn} and the servants had kindled a fire in the middle of the courtyard. {Lk} Peter sat among them, warming himself.

A servant girl of the high priest came by. {Mk} John says it was the girl at the door: “You are not also one of this Man’s disciples, are you?” {Jn} Seeing Peter in the firelight, she looked intently at him and said, “You also were with Jesus of Nazareth.” {Mk} He denied it before them all: “Woman, I do not know Him.” {Lk} Then he went out to the gateway, {Mt} and a rooster crowed. {Mk}

There another girl saw him and told those standing by, “This fellow also was with Jesus of Nazareth.” {Mt} Others took it up: “You also are of them.” {Lk} “You are not also one of His disciples, are you?” {Jn} Again he denied it, this time with an oath: “I do not know the Man!” {Mt}

About an hour later {Lk} the bystanders pressed him again: “Surely you are one of them; for you are a Galilean, and your speech shows it.” {Mk} A servant of the high priest, a relative of the man whose ear Peter had cut off, said, “Did I not see you in the garden with Him?” {Jn} Then Peter began to curse and swear, “I do not know this Man of whom you speak!” {Mk}

Immediately, while he was still speaking, the rooster crowed, {Lk} a second time. {Mk} And the Lord turned and looked at Peter. Peter remembered the word Jesus had said to him, {Lk} “Before the rooster crows twice, you will deny Me three times.” {Mk} He went out and wept bitterly.
differences: The first question comes from the girl who kept the door in John, and from a servant girl by the fire in Matthew, Mark and Luke.
At the second denial Matthew has another girl speak, Mark has the same girl again, Luke has a man (“Man, I am not!”), and John has several people (“they said to him”).
John separates the first denial from the other two with the hearing before Annas; the other Gospels tell all three together.
Only Mark says the rooster crowed twice, matching Jesus’ warning in Mark. Only Luke records the hour between the second and third denials and the Lord turning to look at Peter.
Matthew and Mark say Peter’s Galilean speech gave him away; only John mentions the relative of the man whose ear Peter cut off.

fit.question: The Gospels differ over who challenged Peter and where: a girl at the door or by the fire, then another girl, the same girl, a man, or a group. And Mark alone says the rooster crowed twice. How do the accounts fit?

points.label: Several voices each time
points.text: Each denial answered a challenge, but in a crowded courtyard at night one person would start and others join in. Mark’s girl “began to say to those who stood by” (Mark 14:69). Another girl, a man and a group can all belong to the second round. The third came from “those who stood by” (Matthew, Mark), with Malchus’s relative among them (John).

points.label: Door, fire and gateway
points.text: The doorkeeper let Peter in (John) and later saw him by the fire (Mark, Luke). Peter then moved toward the gateway (Matthew, Mark) and was back by the fire when he was questioned again (John 18:25). The places shift because Peter was trying to slip away.

points.label: One crow or two
points.text: Mark records two crowings and Jesus’ warning with “twice” (Mark 14:30). Mark’s Gospel is traditionally linked to Peter’s own preaching. Matthew, Luke and John mention only the crow that mattered, the one after the third denial. “Before the rooster crows” does not rule out an earlier crow.

fit.note: These are the differences we expect from witnesses to a confused scene at night. On what matters all four agree: three denials, before the rooster crowed, just as Jesus said.
fit.short: Several people challenged Peter each time as he moved between door, fire and gateway. Mark notes two crowings; the others mention the decisive one.

scene.label: The courtyard
scene.text: Large houses were built around an open courtyard, entered through a gateway with a doorkeeper. Rooms opened onto it, some raised above it; Mark says Peter was “below in the courtyard.” From a room or a passage overlooking the yard, Jesus could have seen Peter by the fire. Annas and Caiaphas may well have had quarters in the same palace around one courtyard, as McGarvey thought; that would explain how John can set the denials during the hearing before Annas while the other Gospels set them during the trial before Caiaphas.

scene.label: Galilean speech
scene.text: Galileans spoke Aramaic with a different accent from Jerusalem’s, and later Jewish writings poke fun at how they pronounced some letters. Peter could deny Jesus with his words, but his voice told the truth.

scene.label: The rooster
scene.text: Mark lists “the crowing of the rooster” among the watches of the night (Mark 13:35), the stretch before dawn. Most take Jesus’ words to mean a real bird; a few have suggested the trumpet call that ended the Roman night watch. Either way, the crowing came before dawn.

scene.label: “Curse and swear”
scene.text: This was more than rough language. Peter called down a curse, probably on himself, if he was lying, and he swore an oath. A few hours earlier he had said, “Even if I have to die with You, I will not deny You!” (Matthew 26:35).

witnesses.matthew: Shows each denial worse than the last: a plain denial, then an oath, then curses and swearing. Matthew places it right after the guards mocked Jesus with “Prophesy!”, and soon after it he tells the end of Judas, the other disciple who failed Jesus that night.
witnesses.mark: Is the most exact about the rooster: it crows twice, just as Jesus warned in Mark 14:30. Early church tradition says Mark wrote down Peter’s preaching; if so, Peter told this story against himself, with every detail kept.
witnesses.luke: Alone records that “the Lord turned and looked at Peter,” and the hour between the second and third denials. Luke had already recorded Jesus’ words to Peter at the supper: “I have prayed for you, that your faith should not fail” (22:32).
witnesses.john: Splits the denials around the hearing before Annas and names the doorkeeper, the other disciple and Malchus’s relative. John mentions the “fire of coals” here, a word he uses only once more, for the fire by the lake where the risen Jesus asks Peter three times, “Do you love Me?” (John 21:9, 15–17).

seeing.reveals: Jesus knew Peter’s failure in advance and foretold it to the rooster’s crow. Yet He did not turn away from Peter; He turned toward him, and His word brought Peter to tears rather than to despair.
seeing.living: Peter’s fall did not start with a curse. It started with following at a distance and sitting down among those who did not love Jesus. The way back started when he remembered the word of the Lord. When you have failed Him, go back to what He has said. Jesus foretold Peter’s fall and, in the same breath, spoke of his return (Luke 22:32).
seeing.ponder: When you have failed Jesus, do you hide from His gaze, or let it bring you to tears and back to Him?

preaching.big_idea: Peter failed exactly as Jesus said, and the Lord who foretold his fall turned and looked at him.
preaching.watch_for: In verse 61 Luke twice calls Jesus “the Lord,” at the very moment Peter has said he does not know Him (vv. 57, 60). The Man Peter denied is the Lord, and His word comes true to the letter.

title: Peter Denies Jesus Three Times
